question: In the lecture, it was stated that for a continuous function \(f\) on a closed and bounded interval \([a,b]\), the image \(f([a,b])\) is a closed bounded interval \([d,e]\) where \(d\) is the absolute minimum and \(e\) is the absolute maximum of \(f\). Explain why the image must be closed and bounded, and how the points \(d\) and \(e\) are determined.
answer: Because \([a,b]\) is compact and \(f\) is continuous, the image \(f([a,b])\) is compact in \(\mathbb{R}\). Compact subsets of \(\mathbb{R}\) are precisely the closed and bounded intervals, so \(f([a,b])\) must be closed and bounded. The extreme value theorem guarantees that a continuous function on a compact interval attains its maximum and minimum. Thus there exist points \(x_{\min},x_{\max}\in[a,b]\) such that \(f(x_{\min})=d\) and \(f(x_{\max})=e\). These values \(d\) and \(e\) are the absolute minimum and maximum of \(f\) on \([a,b]\), and the image interval is \([d,e]\).

question: In the lecture, it was stated that any odd polynomial has at least one real root. Explain how the Bolzano Intermediate Value Theorem guarantees this, and then describe how the Fundamental Theorem of Algebra accounts for the remaining roots of the polynomial.
answer: For an odd‑degree polynomial \(f(x)\), the limits \(\lim_{x\to\infty}f(x)=+\infty\) and \(\lim_{x\to-\infty}f(x)=-\infty\) (or vice versa) guarantee that \(f\) takes both positive and negative values. By the Bolzano Intermediate Value Theorem, a continuous function that changes sign on an interval must cross zero somewhere, so \(f\) has at least one real root. The Fundamental Theorem of Algebra then tells us that a polynomial of degree \(n\) has exactly \(n\) complex roots counted with multiplicity. Since at least one of those roots is real, the remaining \(n-1\) roots may be complex (occurring in conjugate pairs if the coefficients are real). Thus the odd polynomial has one real root guaranteed by BIVT, and the total number of roots—including complex ones—is exactly its degree.

\]

Finally, \\(\\forall x\\in S\\) ensures that the implication holds for all points in the domain. Thus, the same \\(\\delta\\) cannot be used for all \\(\\epsilon\\) or all points; it must be chosen anew for each pair \\((\\epsilon,c)\\). This dependence is crucial when proving continuity on a set \\(S\\) because we must verify the epsilon‑delta condition at every point of \\(S\\), and the appropriate \\(\\delta\\) may differ from point to point. question: In the lecture, it was noted that $f(x)=x^2$ is uniformly continuous on the closed interval $[0,1]$ but not on all of $\mathbb{R}$. Explain, using the definition of uniform continuity, why this is the case, and illustrate how the growth of $x^2$ causes the failure of uniform continuity on $\mathbb{R}$.
answer:
On a closed bounded interval such as $[0,1]$ the function $f(x)=x^2$ is Lipschitz.  Its derivative $f'(x)=2x$ is bounded by $2$ on $[0,1]$, so for any $\varepsilon>0$ we can choose $\delta=\varepsilon/2$.  Then for all $x,y\in[0,1]$ with $|x-y|<\delta$ we have 
$$|f(x)-f(y)|=|x^2-y^2|=|x-y||x+y|\le |x-y|\cdot 2<2\delta=\varepsilon,$$ 
which satisfies the definition of uniform continuity.

On the whole real line this argument fails because the derivative is unbounded.  For any fixed $\delta>0$ we can pick $x$ large enough so that $|x-(x+\delta/2)|<\delta$ but 
$$|f(x)-f(x+\delta/2)|=|x^2-(x+\delta/2)^2|=|x^2-(x^2+x\delta+x^2/4)|=x\delta+\delta^2/4>1$$ 
when $x> rac{1}{\delta}$.  Thus for $\varepsilon=1$ no single $\delta$ works for all $x\in\mathbb{R}$, and $f$ is not uniformly continuous on $\mathbb{R}$.

Uniform continuity requires a single \(\delta>0\) that works for *all* points in the domain for a given \(\varepsilon>0\). question: In the lecture, it is claimed that a function \(F\) is uniformly continuous on a closed and bounded interval \(A\subseteq\mathbb{R}\) if and only if it is continuous on \(A\). answer: The equivalence relies on the fact that on a closed and bounded interval \(A\) (hence compact), continuity of \(F\) guarantees that for every \(\varepsilon>0\) the pre‑image of the open interval \((F(x)-\varepsilon,F(x)+\varepsilon)\) is an open set covering \(A\). By compactness, a finite subcover exists, yielding a single \(\delta>0\) that works for all points in \(A\); this is precisely the definition of uniform continuity. The closed and bounded hypothesis is essential because on an unbounded set the same argument fails: for \(F(x)=1/x\) on \((0,1]\) the function is continuous but not uniformly continuous, as \(\delta\) would have to shrink to zero near \(0\); similarly \(F(x)=x^2\) on \(\mathbb{R}\) is continuous but not uniformly continuous because the slope grows without bound. Replacing \(A\) by any compact set \(K\subseteq\mathbb{R}\) preserves the argument: compactness still supplies a finite subcover of the open sets \(\{x\in K:\,|F(x)-F(y)|<\varepsilon\}\) for each \(y\), giving a global \(\delta\). The Bolzano–Weierstrass theorem enters the proof of the converse direction (uniform continuity \(\Rightarrow\) continuity) by providing a convergent subsequence when assuming a failure of continuity. If \(F\) were not continuous at some \(x_0\in K\), one could construct sequences \(x_n\to x_0\) with \(|F(x_n)-F(x_0)|\ge\varepsilon\). Compactness ensures a convergent subsequence \(x_{n_k}\to x'\in K\); uniform continuity would then force \(|F(x_{n_k})-F(x')|<\varepsilon/2\) for large \(k\), contradicting the construction. Thus Bolzano–Weierstrass guarantees the existence of the necessary convergent subsequence, completing the proof that on a compact set continuity and uniform continuity are equivalent.
